keys: Attribute owner (the object that decides the set)
How a category gets an attribute

Amazon.How a category gets an attribute: a name-PK Attribute + a ProductTypeAttribute join {marketplaceId, parentageLevel, required} — 213 types → 208 attributes, 1,154 pairs; the join is mutable (15,299 of 26,135 flavour release-note rows are “deleted and no longer associated”).
Amazon.Value list scope: per (ProductType, marketplace) schema — a soft enum (free string schema-valid, suggested list alongside); on the legacy XSD surface definitions diverge per type (101–124 names with differing maxLength).
Amazon.Stated why: none stated. Inference: a schema is compiled per (type × marketplace × parentage level) with monthly deltas; a stable name lets it regenerate without invalidating stored values.

Shopify.Attribute owner (the object that decides: two surfaces: the taxonomy (TaxonomyCategory.attributes) and MetafieldDefinition with category constraints.
Shopify.How a category gets an attribute: taxonomy: a category→attribute edge (93,007) to a global attribute (8,240 base; 316 extended aliases reuse the base GID); metafields: constraints {key: "category", values: […]} on one definition (7,750 ids on shopify.color-pattern).
Shopify.Value list scope: global per attribute — a TaxonomyValue belongs to exactly one attribute (0 of 74,820 shared); live: Flavor 1458 has the same 30 values on every node that carries it. Different vocabularies = different types (Flavor 293 categories · Pet food flavor 54 · Baby food flavor 4 · E-liquid flavor 10).
Shopify.Stated why: for the constraint: “some metafield definitions should only apply to a subset of resources … Shoe size … wouldn't apply to Sweaters.” Nothing on why the taxonomy attribute is global.

Google.How a category gets an attribute: it doesn't; the category gates requiredness (and availability for 3).
Google.Stated why: none. Inference: a flat feed from sellers Google does not control; a per-category schema would force every seller to resolve a taxonomy node before serialising a row.

eBay.How a category gets an attribute: each leaf's aspect list is materialised in full — 197,046 aspects over 15,111 leaves; the same category id under two trees returns two different lists.
eBay.Value list scope: per leaf (aspectValues on the constraint; FREE_TEXT on 156,337).
eBay.Identity of the attribute: none — aspectId 0, valueId 0; identified only by localizedAspectName within the category.
eBay.Stated why: none. Inference: aspect lists are versioned per (tree, category, marketplace); per-leaf materialisation lets a set change without a global migration.

Walmart.Attribute owner (the object that decides: the product type (a flat map of 6,967).
Walmart.How a category gets an attribute: written out in full per type — 6,576 names × 383,947 slots; 1,767 names have more than one definition (flavor 50, color 126, size 438).
Walmart.Value list scope: per type (enum in the slot); for flavor 0 of 6,967 types close the list.
Walmart.Identity of the attribute: the slot name inside the type ($ref 0).
Walmart.Stated why: the consequence only: “Based on the chosen Product Type, attribute requirements, values, and recommendations will vary.”

Shopee.How a category gets an attribute: per leaf; whether an attribute_id is shared across categories or re-minted per category is open (U-8).
Shopee.Value list scope: on the attribute — search_attribute_value_list keyed by attribute_id alone.
Shopee.Stated why: none; no attribute inventory is published.

Tokopedia.Attribute owner (the object that decides: the leaf category (Era B: GET …/categories/{id}/attributes; Era A: get_variant?cat_id= + Annotations).
Tokopedia.How a category gets an attribute: bound per category; the “Imported Goods” attribute is one id (102254) with one value pair across every category but digital — one route.
Tokopedia.Identity of the attribute: id: string (Era B); Era A's Annotation group has no stable id.
Tokopedia.Stated why: operational only: “Use the Get Attributes to check what attributes are mandatory.”

Square.Attribute owner (the object that decides: the object type (allowed_object_types), not the category.
Square.How a category gets an attribute: it doesn't — “that definition is available for all objects of that type.”
Square.Stated why: none. Inference: single-tenant tooling; the 10+10 cap removes the problem scoping would solve.

Salesforce B2C.Attribute owner (the object that decides: the object type + attribute groups attached to the classification category.
Salesforce B2C.How a category gets an attribute: an ObjectAttributeGroup is attached to a category; “Attributes can belong to more than one attribute group”; the model unions global + classification category + its ancestors.
Salesforce B2C.Stated why: “to help you manage product attributes”; inference: a merchant-owned tree, so inheritance costs nothing.

Akeneo.How a category gets an attribute: it doesn't (0 hits over 344 files); a family subscribes: “Several families of products can use the same attributes.”
Akeneo.Stated why: “The family helps managing the product's completeness as you can say at the family level, which family attributes are required for the completeness calculation.”

WooCommerce.Attribute owner (the object that decides: none — a store-global registry applied to any product.
WooCommerce.How a category gets an attribute: it doesn't (six registry columns, none references a category).
WooCommerce.Value list scope: on the attribute (global terms) or on the product (local attributes).
WooCommerce.Stated why: “Attributes can be defined globally, so they’re easy to update across the entire store, and available to be used on any product, or … defined individually, at the product level.” — the only explicit rationale for globality.

commercetools.How a category gets an attribute: it doesn't; a definition is nested in its ProductType (“not a resource”); the same name across types must share a type.
commercetools.Value list scope: per ProductType — “the enum values can be different for each ProductType”.
commercetools.Identity of the attribute: name — unique “within the Project” (resource doc) vs “within the ProductType” (draft doc): open contradiction U6.
commercetools.Stated why: “You wouldn't ask for the Neckline of a pair of jeans, would you? By defining appropriate Attribute types for each Product Type, you prevent irrelevant or nonsensical data from being entered.”

Magento.How a category gets an attribute: it doesn't — the browse category plays no part in any schema table; sets subscribe via eav_entity_attribute (attribute_set_id, attribute_group_id, attribute_id).
Magento.Value list scope: on the attribute — eav_attribute_option; the running store holds the union of two fixtures' size lists (20 options).
Magento.Stated why: the set's purpose: “The attribute set determines the fields that are available during data entry, and the values that appear to the customer.”
